title: YOU CANNOT SERVE GOD AND MONEY: THE SENTENCE THAT EXPOSES WHO REALLY OWNS YOUR HEART
paragraphs: YOU CANNOT SERVE GOD AND MONEY: THE SENTENCE THAT EXPOSES WHO REALLY OWNS YOUR HEART
Jesus was never afraid of your money. He was after something far more dangerous—the throne your money may be sitting on.
There is a question most Christians would answer correctly in public.
“Who is your Lord?”
Jesus.
Of course Jesus.
But there is another question that is much harder to answer.
What do you run to when you are afraid?
What makes you feel secure?
What loss would make you feel as though your entire life were collapsing?
What occupies your imagination when you cannot sleep?
What are you willing to compromise to obtain?
And what do you secretly believe would finally make you feel safe, important, successful, respected, or free?
Because sometimes the mouth says, “Jesus is Lord,” while the nervous system whispers, “But I need more money before I can breathe.”
Sometimes we sing about surrender on Sunday and spend Monday terrified because a number on a screen moved in the wrong direction.
Sometimes we do not bow before golden statues.
We bow before salaries.
Savings.
Promotions.
Possessions.
Business opportunities.
Status.
The fear of not having enough.
And sometimes the idol is not wealth itself.
Sometimes it is the promise we think wealth makes:
I can protect you.
I can make people respect you.
I can make sure you never have to depend on anyone.
I can give you control.
Then Jesus walks directly into that hidden place and says something so uncompromising that there is almost no comfortable way around it:
“No one can serve two masters.”
The Greek of Matthew 6:24 is even worth slowing down for:
“Οὐδεὶς δύναται δυσὶ κυρίοις δουλεύειν … οὐ δύνασθε θεῷ δουλεύειν καὶ μαμωνᾷ.”
Oudeis dynatai dysi kyriois douleuein … ou dynasthe Theō douleuein kai mamōna.
In straightforward English:
“No one is able to serve two masters … You are not able to serve God and mammon.”
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not merely say that serving both is difficult.
He says you cannot do it.

The Greek verb δουλεύειν (douleuein) comes from the language of serving as a slave or bondservant. Jesus is therefore talking about something deeper than possessing money, earning money, saving money, investing money, running a business, or providing for your family.
He is talking about mastery.
Who owns your allegiance?
Who gets the final word?
Who determines what you love?
Who controls what you fear?
Who defines whether your life is successful?
That is why this verse is not fundamentally a condemnation of currency.
It is an exposure of worship.
Money can sit in your bank account without sitting on the throne of your heart.
And a person can have very little money while being completely ruled by the desire for it.
A wealthy believer can hold possessions with an open hand.
A poor believer can obsess over wealth with a clenched heart.
The issue Jesus exposes is not simply what is in your hand.
It is what has your heart.
And that makes His warning uncomfortable for nearly everyone.
Because mammon does not always enter your life wearing the face of greed.
Sometimes it arrives disguised as responsibility.
“I just need a little more.”
Then a little more becomes the next amount.
And the next.
And the next.
You finally earn what you once prayed for, but peace still does not come.
So you move the finish line.
“When I make this much…”
“When the business reaches this level…”
“When I own the house…”
“When the debt disappears…”
“When my savings reach this number…”
“When I finally have enough…”
Enough.
That may be one of the most revealing words in our relationship with money.
Because if God does not define “enough,” appetite will.
And appetite has no finish line.

Jesus' statement also comes in a context that matters. In Matthew 6, He speaks about treasures on earth and treasures in heaven. He speaks about the eye and the condition of the inner person. Then He speaks about two masters. Immediately afterward, He addresses anxiety about food, drink, and clothing and calls His disciples to seek first God's kingdom and righteousness.
That means Matthew 6:24 cannot honestly be reduced to, “Rich people are bad.”
Jesus is reaching much deeper.
Treasure.
Vision.
Mastery.
Anxiety.
Trust.
Kingdom.
They are connected.
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).
Your spending can reveal something about your heart.
Your giving can reveal something about your heart.
Your anxiety can reveal something about your heart.
Your unwillingness to release something when God calls you to obedience can reveal something about your heart.
Your financial success can reveal something about your heart.
Your financial suffering can reveal something about your heart.
Money has a strange ability to uncover loyalties we did not know were there.
And perhaps that is why Jesus speaks about it so sharply.
Because money makes an extraordinary servant.
But it makes a terrible god.
Money can buy medicine.
It cannot command another heartbeat.
Money can purchase a bed.
It cannot guarantee sleep.
Money can build a beautiful house.
It cannot create a faithful marriage.
Money can buy attention.
It cannot purchase genuine love.
Money can hire security.
It cannot forgive your sins.
Money can place your name on buildings.
It cannot write your name in the Book of Life.
Money can make people recognize you when you enter a room.
It cannot make heaven recognize you as righteous before God.
And one day every dollar, peso, pound, euro, property title, investment account, possession, award, and status symbol will remain on this side of eternity.
Paul makes essentially this point in 1 Timothy 6:
“We brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world.”
Then comes another frequently misunderstood warning.
The Greek text of 1 Timothy 6:10 begins:
“ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία…”
The crucial word is φιλαργυρία (philargyria).
It means love of money or avarice.

Paul is not saying that physical money itself is inherently evil. His warning concerns a heart captured by the love and craving of wealth. The surrounding passage warns about the desire to become rich and describes people being drawn into temptation, destructive desires, and spiritual ruin.
Then comes the terrifying image:
Some, craving money, “wandered away from the faith” and “pierced themselves with many sorrows.”
Read that slowly.
They pierced themselves.
That is what idols eventually do.
They make promises they cannot keep and then wound the people who trusted them.
Mammon says:
“Give me your life and I will give you security.”
So you give it your time.
Your marriage.
Your integrity.
Your attention.
Your sleep.
Your children.
Your convictions.
Your worship.
Your health.
Your conscience.
Your years.
And after collecting everything, mammon still cannot guarantee that tomorrow will arrive.
Jesus, however, offers something money never can.
Himself.
This is where Christianity becomes radically different from mere moral advice.
The Gospel is not simply Jesus telling greedy people to become generous enough that God will accept them.
If that were the Gospel, none of us would survive it.
Because greed is only one symptom of the deeper rebellion Scripture calls sin.
We have all wanted created things more than the Creator.
Money may be your rival master.
For someone else, it may be sex.
Approval.
Power.
Beauty.
Achievement.
Comfort.
Politics.
Family.
Reputation.
Even ministry can become an idol when being seen doing something for Jesus becomes more precious than Jesus Himself.
The scandal is not merely that human beings worship money.
The scandal is that sinners repeatedly exchange the glory of God for created things—and yet God moved toward sinners in mercy.
Jesus Christ came.
Not as another financial guru promising the secret to prosperity.
Not as a motivational speaker teaching us how to manifest abundance.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He loved the Father perfectly.
He obeyed where we rebelled.
He resisted every rival throne.
And then Christ went willingly to the cross.
There the sinless One bore judgment for sinners.
The greedy.
The proud.
The fraudulent.
The materialistic.
The anxious.
The self-righteous.
The financially broken person who thinks poverty automatically makes him holy.
The wealthy person whose possessions quietly became his identity.
People like us.
Jesus was crucified, buried, and raised.
And suddenly the question is no longer merely:
“How much money do you have?”
The far greater question becomes:
“Who has you?”
Because Christianity is not Jesus becoming one priority among several.
Jesus is Lord.
That title changes everything.
Your money becomes His.
Your career becomes His.
Your business becomes His.
Your possessions become His.
Your ambitions become His.
Your future becomes His.
Even your fears must eventually kneel before Him.
This does not mean Christians should become irresponsible with money.
Quite the opposite.

Scripture commends work, provision, wisdom, generosity, stewardship, contentment, and care for others. Paul later tells wealthy believers in the same chapter of 1 Timothy not to become arrogant or place their hope in uncertain riches, but in God, and to be rich in good works and generosity.
The biblical answer to money is therefore neither worship nor careless rejection.
It is stewardship under the lordship of Christ.
You may own something without allowing it to own you.
You may earn without worshiping earnings.
You may save without placing your hope in savings.
You may succeed without making success your identity.
You may enjoy God's provision while remembering that the gift must never replace the Giver.
And sometimes God exposes our attachment by asking us to open our hands.
That is where things become personal.
Because generosity sounds beautiful until it costs something.
Surrender sounds powerful until God touches the thing you wanted to control.
Trust sounds spiritual until the numbers frighten you.
Then the heart begins negotiating.
“Lord, You can have everything…”
Except this.
And whatever follows the word except deserves examination.
Not automatic condemnation.
Examination.
Because Jesus does not expose idols merely to humiliate us.
He exposes them to free us.
Perhaps you have spent years chasing money because you grew up without it.
You remember the embarrassment.
The unpaid bills.
The arguments behind closed doors.
The fear when rent was due.
The feeling of watching other children receive what your family could not afford.
So somewhere deep inside, you made a vow.
I will never live like that again.
You worked.
You sacrificed.
You became disciplined.
None of those things is necessarily sinful.
But slowly, almost invisibly, financial security became emotional salvation.
You stopped simply earning money.
You started asking money to heal the frightened child inside you.
But money cannot do that.
Maybe your story is different.
Perhaps money became proof that you mattered.
Every promotion whispered, “You are somebody.”
Every expensive purchase told the world, “Look how far I have come.”
Every compliment about your success gave you another temporary dose of significance.
But then somebody became richer.
Somebody bought something better.
Somebody passed you.
And suddenly your peace disappeared.
That is the cruelty of comparison.
There will almost always be someone with more.
More followers.
More money.
More property.
More influence.
More success.
More applause.
If your identity depends upon outrunning everyone else, you can never rest.
Jesus offers something infinitely better.
An identity you do not have to purchase.
Grace you cannot earn.
Forgiveness you cannot finance.
A kingdom you cannot buy your way into.
A Father whose love is not auctioned to the highest bidder.
You come empty-handed.
That is humiliating to human pride.
And unbelievably beautiful.
At the cross, billionaires and beggars arrive the same way.
Needing mercy.
No VIP entrance.
No premium salvation package.
No amount of wealth can purchase justification before a holy God.
Christ paid the price we could never pay.
That is grace.
And grace begins rewriting our relationship with everything.
Including money.
From clutching to surrender.
From greed to generosity.
From anxiety to trust.
From accumulation as identity to stewardship as worship.
From “This is mine” to “Lord, how would You have me use what You entrusted to me?”
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So perhaps the question today is not, “Am I rich?”
Perhaps the question is:
If Jesus asked for complete lordship over my finances, would I secretly resent Him?
Do not rush past that.
Sit with it.
What happens inside you when you imagine giving generously?
What happens when obedience threatens profit?
What happens when integrity costs you money?
What happens when somebody else's blessing exceeds yours?
What happens when God does not increase your income according to your timetable?
What happens when you have enough for today but not enough to control tomorrow?
Those reactions can become windows into the heart.
Maybe you have been calling Jesus “Lord” while asking money to be your savior.
If that realization hurts, do not run from Christ.
Run to Him.
Repentance is not God standing at a distance shouting, “Fix yourself.”
Repentance is turning from the false master toward the true King.
Confess the greed.
Confess the envy.
Confess the financial dishonesty.
Confess the obsession with appearances.
Confess the fear.
Confess the way possessions became identity.
Confess the way success became your measurement of human worth.
Bring it into the light.
There is mercy at the cross.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could become better at hiding.
He died and rose so sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, transformed, and made free.
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, you can simply pray:

“Jesus Christ, You are Lord. Forgive me for trusting created things more than I have trusted You. Forgive my greed, fear, pride, envy, and unbelief. Everything I possess came under Your sovereign hand, and everything I am belongs to You. Teach me to work faithfully, steward wisely, give generously, live contentedly, and trust You completely. Tear every rival throne out of my heart. I do not want money to be my master. I want You. Thank You for the cross. Thank You for Your mercy. Thank You that Your grace is greater than my sin. Change me from the inside out. Amen.”

And maybe somebody needs to make that confession publicly—not because commenting earns forgiveness, because it absolutely does not, but because there are moments when bringing a struggle into the light becomes the beginning of honest Christian community.
No pretending.
There may be another believer reading the comments who understands exactly what that battle feels like.

And if Christ has already been teaching you freedom from greed, fear, or financial idolatry, tell us what He has taught you. Your testimony may become the sentence another struggling believer desperately needed tonight.
Then think of one person who needs this truth.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Someone you love.
Salvation cannot be purchased, and God's favor is never for sale.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can help that work continue reaching people with Scripture, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and the message of Jesus Christ.
More importantly, we want this community to become something deeper than content consumption.
A place where Scripture confronts us.
Grace restores us.
Truth sharpens us.
And Jesus remains the center.
Not because every sentence will feel urgent today.
Or the financial crisis.
Or the opportunity to compromise.
Or the frightening bank statement.
Or unexpected prosperity.
And on that day you may need to remember what Jesus said before your fear or ambition starts preaching another gospel to you.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to purchase a blessing.
Not because clicking “Share” makes anyone righteous.
Somebody may be working themselves to death trying to become valuable.
Somebody may have plenty in the bank and nothing resembling peace in the soul.
Somebody may be terrified because they have almost nothing left.
Both need the same ultimate hope.
Not more mammon.
Christ.
Because when everything temporary is stripped away, the greatest treasure God gives His people is not a larger account, a bigger house, a more successful business, or a painless life.
It is Jesus Himself.
And if you have Christ, you possess a treasure death itself cannot confiscate.
So examine your heart tonight.
Who is your master?
What do you trust?
What are you terrified to lose?
What has been promising you salvation while quietly demanding your worship?
Bring it to Jesus.
Open the clenched fist.
Repent.
Receive grace.
And remember:
Money can leave your hands in a moment—but nothing can bankrupt the soul whose treasure is Christ.
